cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: So, Rosie and Martin, let’s look at what you’ve got for your presentation on woolly mammoths.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: OK, we’ve got a short outline here.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: Thanks. So it’s about a research project in North America?

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Yes. But we thought we needed something general about woolly mammoths in our introduction, to establish that they were related to our modern elephant, and they lived thousands of years ago in the last ice age.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: Maybe we could show a video clip of a cartoon about mammoths. But that’d be a bit childish. Or we could have a diagram, (Q21) it could be a timeline to show when they lived, with illustrations?

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Or we could just show a drawing of them walking in the ice? No, let’s go with your last suggestion.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: Good. Then you’re describing the discovery of the mammoth tooth on St Paul’s Island in Alaska, and why it was significant.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: Yes. The tooth was found by a man called Russell Graham. He picked it up from under a rock in a cave. He knew it was special – for a start it was in really good condition, as if it had been just extracted from the animal’s jawbone. Anyway, they found it was 6,500 years old.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: So why was that significant?

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: Well (Q22) the mammoth bones previously found on the North American mainland were much less recent than that. So this was really amazing.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Then we’re making an animated diagram to show the geography of the area in prehistoric times. So originally, St Paul’s Island wasn’t an island, it was connected to the mainland, and mammoths and other animals like bears were able to roam around the whole area.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: Then the climate warmed up and the sea level began to rise, and the island got cut off from the mainland. So (Q23) those mammoths on the island couldn’t escape; they had to stay on the island.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: And in fact the species survived there for thousands of years after they’d become extinct on the mainland.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: So why do you think they died out on the mainland?

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: No one’s sure.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Anyway, next we’ll explain how Graham and his team identified the date when the mammoths became extinct on the island. They concluded that (Q24) the extinction happened 5,600 years ago, which is a very precise time for a prehistoric extinction. It’s based on samples they took from mud at the bottom of a lake on the island. They analysed it to find out what had fallen in over time – bits of plants, volcanic ash and even DNA from the mammoths themselves. It’s standard procedure, but it took nearly two years to do.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: So why don’t you quickly go through the main sections of your presentation and discuss what action’s needed for each part?

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: OK. So for the introduction, we’re using a visual, so once we’ve prepared that we’re done.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: I’m not sure. I think (Q25) we need to write down all the ideas we want to include here, not just rely on memory. How we begin the presentation is so important …

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: You’re right.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: The discovery of the mammoth tooth is probably the most dramatic part, but we don’t have that much information, only what we got from the online article. I thought maybe (Q26) we could get in touch with the researcher who led the team and ask him to tell us a bit more.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Great idea. What about the section with the initial questions asked by the researchers? We’ve got a lot on that but we need to make it interesting.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: We could (Q27) ask the audience to suggest some questions about it and then see how many of them we can answer. I don’t think it would take too long.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: Yes that would add a bit of variety.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Then the section on further research carried out on the island – analysing the mud in the lake. I wonder if we’ve actually got too much information here, should we cut some?

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: I don’t think so, but it’s all a bit muddled at present.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: Yes, (Q28) maybe it would be better if it followed a chronological pattern.

cues.speaker: ROSIE
cues.text: I think so. The findings and possible explanations section is just about ready, but we need to practice it (Q29) so we’re sure it won’t overrun.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: I think it should be OK, but yes, let’s make sure.

cues.speaker: TUTOR
cues.text: In the last section, relevance to the present day, you’ve got some good ideas but this is where you need to move away from the ideas of others and (Q30) give your own viewpoint.

cues.speaker: MARTIN
cues.text: OK, we’ll think about that. Now shall we …
